Whether a Family's Expected Information Is Written Out

Source: R/generics.R, R/numerical_fallbacks.R
expected_hessian_exact.Rd

Returns TRUE when the family computes its expected information exactly, in closed form or by a quadrature of its own to working precision, and FALSE when a call to distrib_expected_hessian() reaches a fallback and the answer is therefore an approximation. It is a generic so that a family whose registered method is not what its owning class suggests can report this; has_exact_expected_hessian() calls it and expected_hessian_exact.distrib() is the default.

Implements the test that has_exact_expected_hessian() applies, as a generic so that a family whose registered method differs from what its owning class indicates can supply its own answer.

Usage

expected_hessian_exact(x, ...)

Arguments

x

An object inheriting from class "distrib".

...

Passed to methods.

Value

A single logical.

A single logical.

Details

A function that reports the information of a family uses the predicate to choose which information to report. Where it returns TRUE the expected information costs one evaluation and has the smaller variance, so it is the better matrix to invert; where it returns FALSE the choice is between an approximation and the observed Hessian, which every family has and which is exact. fit_distrib() follows this rule for its standard errors, and statmodels7 follows it in vcov().

Every shipped univariate family returns TRUE. The Poisson-inverse Gaussian families sum their expected information exactly over the support, and the skew normals, the skew t and the pseudo-Huber evaluate one quadrature over the standardized response per distinct shape; see loc_scale_expected(). Among the wrappers, truncated() returns FALSE.

Reading the class that owns the registered method is not sufficient on its own, and the generic exists for this reason: a method registered on the class of a family may chain onto a parent that approximates, and a family that does so returns the answer of its parent.

The default reads the class on which the distrib_expected_hessian() method is registered: the base classes carry the approximating method and every other registration is, by default, a family that wrote the expectation out.

Reading the owner is not sufficient in general. A method registered on the class of a family may be a chain onto a parent that approximates, and then the owner reads as "written out" although the arithmetic is not. A family that chains onto another therefore returns the answer of its parent, as the wrappers do; truncated() returns FALSE unconditionally.

See also

has_exact_expected_hessian(), the wrapper that calls it; distrib_expected_hessian() for the quantity itself, and expected_by_opg() for the fallback that a FALSE answer reaches.

has_exact_expected_hessian(), distrib_dexpected_hessian()

Examples

# A Gaussian writes its information out; a truncated Gaussian does not.
expected_hessian_exact(gaussian1_distrib())
#> [1] TRUE
expected_hessian_exact(truncated(gaussian1_distrib(), lower = 0))
#> [1] FALSE
